title: Preface
summary: Describes a declassified CIA history excerpt on the establishment of the U-2 project (Project AQUATONE). It covers Allen Dulles assigning Richard Bissell in November 1954 to run the high-altitude reconnaissance overflight program; a Pentagon meeting with Air Force officials (Trevor Gardner, Gen. Donald Putt) about diverting Pratt & Whitney J57 engines and funding Lockheed airframes; funding via the Contingency Reserve Fund; staff buildup including administrator James Cunningham; and the project's separate, self-sufficient personnel, contracting, and finance structure with its personnel table.

title: S~ORN

nodes.title: S~ORN (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes Project AQUATONE's 1955 staffing of 357 personnel (92 CIA, 109 Air Force, 156 contractors) across headquarters, a US testing facility, and three foreign bases. Traces the project HQ's moves in Washington from 1954 to 1968 (E Street buildings, Quarters Eye on Ohio Drive, then the Matomic Building, then Langley in 1962, and finally OSA in 1968). Notes Bissell reported to the DCI, while Gen. Charles Pearre Cabell, the DDCI, oversaw day-to-day U-2 affairs and attended White House meetings.

nodes.title: FUNDING ARRANGEMENTS FOR PROJECT AQUATONE
nodes.summary: Funding for Project AQUATONE (the U-2): work began before a contract via unvouchered covert funds; Kelly Johnson assembled 25 then 81 Lockheed staff with long workweeks. Public Law 110 lets only the DCI obligate unvouchered funds, avoiding competitive bidding and speeding procurement. Eisenhower authorized $35M from the Contingency Reserve; a Dec 1954 letter contract (Project OARFISH) used performance specs and a fixed price of $22.5M for airframes. Lockheed delivered on time and under budget; final 1958 cost was about $18.98M for 20 aircraft, under $1M each, since the U-2 reused F-104 tooling.

nodes.title: MAJOR DESIGN FEATURES OF THE U-2
nodes.summary: Describes the U-2 reconnaissance aircraft's development at Lockheed's Skunk Works under Kelly Johnson: secrecy, rapid engineer-mechanic collaboration, December 1954 specs (Mach 0.8, ~73,100 ft ceiling, 244 nm glide, 450 lb payload limit, first flight by Aug 1955). Covers design features: fuel and weight challenges, sailplane-derived tail and wing attachment with tension bolts, wings as integral fuel tanks, the gust control mechanism below 35,000 ft, and the skid-landing recovery.

nodes.title: THE DEVELOPMENT OF THE CAMERA SYSTEM
nodes.summary: Describes the development of the U-2's camera system in the 1950s. Early aerial cameras lacked the resolution needed for high-altitude intelligence, which required under 10 feet resolution. James Baker's 1940s high-acuity lens was too heavy. Baker adapted Hycon K-38 cameras into the A-1 (rocking-mount oblique system) and A-2 (trimetrogon with 24-inch aspheric lenses at 60 lines/mm). He then designed the B camera (36-inch lens, 100 lines/mm, panoramic) which became the workhorse, and the C camera (180-inch mirror system), which was shelved in 1957 due to vibration. Also covers Spica Inc., the periscope, and key contractors and dates.

nodes.title: PREPARATIONS FOR TESTING THE U-2
nodes.summary: Describes preparations for testing the U-2 in 1955: the Development Projects Staff searched California and Nevada for a secret test site. On 12 April 1955, Bissell, Ritland, Johnson, and pilot Tony LeVier spotted Groom Lake, a former WWII gunnery airstrip near the AEC Nevada Proving Ground, and nearly landed on its dusty, unsafe strip. The site, later called Area 51 or the Ranch, was given a paved runway and was ready by July 1955.

summary: Project AQUATONE (U-2) in 1955 staffed 357 personnel (92 CIA, 109 Air Force, 156 contractors) across HQ, a test facility, and three foreign bases. HQ moved in Washington from 1954 to 1968. Bissell reported to the DCI; DDCI Cabell oversaw daily U-2 affairs. Funding used unvouchered covert funds and a $35M Contingency Reserve authorization, with a $22.5M fixed-price letter contract (OARFISH); final cost about $18.98M for 20 aircraft. Design covered Skunk Works development under Kelly Johnson, specs, sailplane-derived features, integral wing tanks, gust control, and skid landing. Camera development covered James Baker's A, B, and C cameras, with C shelved in 1957. Groom Lake was chosen as the test site in April 1955 and was ready by July 1955.

title: SECURITY FOR THE U-2 PROJECT
summary: Describes security for the CIA's U-2 overhead reconnaissance project (AQUATONE). After a 1955 agreement, the CIA took primary security responsibility, requiring untraceable contracts, clearance decisions, and physical security at factories. Photos were tightly compartmented, limiting analyst access. Code terms ('articles', 'drivers', KWEXTRA/KWGLITFER) hid the program's nature. Altimeters ordered from Kollman Instrument, which only went to 45,000 feet, were covered by a rocket-plane cover story.

title: THE CIA- AIR FORCE PARTNERSHIP
summary: Describes the CIA-Air Force partnership in the U-2 program: 1954-1955 interagency talks, Dulles-Twining dispute over SAC control resolved by Eisenhower's insistence on a civilian operation, and the 3 August 1955 OILSTONE agreement giving the Air Force selection roles and CIA program control, with Lockheed keeping aircraft construction. Covers Air Force officers Ritland, Gibbs, and Geary and their roles, including Geary's long tenure as focal point for overhead reconnaissance support.

title: TECHNICAL CHALLENGES TO HIGH-ALTITUDE FLIGHT

nodes.title: TECHNICAL CHALLENGES TO HIGH-ALTITUDE FLIGHT (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes Lockheed U-2 high-altitude flight challenges: a special low-vapor-pressure fuel (LF-1A/JP-7, made by Shell, causing a Flit shortage), the physiological danger of boiling blood above 65,000 ft requiring pressure suits, and the MC-2/MC-3 partial-pressure suits developed with David Clark and Firewel, including early discomfort, crashes, and ejection and seat issues. Also covers bailout tests, prebreathing, food, water, urination problems, weight loss, and the suicide L-pill poison ampules offered to pilots.

nodes.title: DELIVERY OF THE FIRST U-2
nodes.summary: Covers the July 1955 delivery of the first U-2 (article 341, 'Kelly's Angel') to Groom Lake, and its Air Force 'utility aircraft' designator chosen to conceal its reconnaissance role. Describes the engine choice: P&W J57-P-31 preferred, but early aircraft used the P-37 (lower thrust, heavier, about 20% less efficient). Details the wet-wing fuel design, 100-gallon nose reserve tank, 1957 slipper tanks, and mechanical fuel totalizer counters used instead of fuel gauges, plus pilot fuel-tracking methods.

nodes.title: INITIAL TESTING OF THE U-2
nodes.summary: Describes initial testing of the Lockheed U-2 in 1955: LeVier's unplanned hop and rough landing on 1 August, minor damage, and the first planned flight on 4 August with Kelly Johnson guiding landings. The official first flight on 8 August reached 32,000 feet. Testing covered stall envelope, 2.5g stress limit, Mach 0.85, 52,000 ft on 16 August, and 65,600 ft on 8 September. Flameouts at high altitude, caused by the P-37 engine's poor combustion, were the "chimney" problem until P-31 engines arrived in spring 1956. Logistics included MATS C-54 shuttle flights from Burbank to Area 51, and a 17 November 1955 crash killed 14 people.

summary: Covers the Lockheed U-2's high-altitude challenges: special LF-1A/JP-7 fuel, boiling-blood danger above 65,000 ft requiring MC-2/MC-3 pressure suits (with discomfort, crashes, ejection issues), bailout tests, prebreathing, food, water, urination, weight loss, and suicide L-pill ampules. Also covers the July 1955 delivery of the first U-2 to Groom Lake, its 'utility aircraft' cover designator, P-37 vs P-31 engines, wet-wing fuel design, tanks, and fuel totalizers. Finally, initial 1955 testing: flights, altitude records to 65,600 ft, flameout 'chimney' problem, MATS logistics, and the 17 November 1955 crash killing 14.

title: U-2s, UFOs, AND OPERATION BLUE BOOK
summary: U-2 high-altitude flights in the mid-1950s caused a surge in UFO reports, since airliners and military aircraft flew at lower altitudes and airliner pilots saw U-2s lit by the sun at high altitude while the planes below were in darkness. Reports went to air-traffic controllers and the Air Force's Operation BLUE BOOK at Wright-Patterson, which checked sightings against Agency U-2 flight logs. This eliminated most reports, though the true cause could not be disclosed. U-2 and OXCART flights accounted for over half of UFO reports in the late 1950s and most of the 1960s.

title: HIRING U-2 PilOTS
summary: Explains that Eisenhower wanted non-US citizen U-2 pilots for deniability. The DDP's initial foreign-pilot effort failed by autumn 1955. Bissell then recruited SAC fighter pilots with reserve commissions, authorized by Lt. Gen. O'Donnell, who had to resign from the Air Force and become civilians ("sheep-dipping"). Pilots were lured by high salaries and promises of return and promotion. CIA screening was stricter than the Air Force's, causing more rejections but yielding a much lower accident rate.

title: PILOT TRAINING

nodes.title: PILOT TRAINING (intro)
nodes.summary: Describes U-2 pilot training: Air Force SAC pilots, supervised by Col. William F. Yancey at March AFB, were trained by Lockheed test pilots (Tony LeVier) at Area 51, with no two-seat trainer for about 15 years. Covers U-2 flight limits (placarded speeds, Mach 0.8), the narrow 'coffin corner' airspeed band at altitude, the vernier throttle, and celestial sextant and periscope navigation with dead-reckoning accuracy under 1 nm per 1,000 nm.

nodes.title: FINAL TESTS OF THE U-2
nodes.summary: Describes the U-2 Project AQUATONE program: the CIA-executed purchase of 31 U-2s for the Air Force (Follow-On Group, FOG), and April 1956 final tests with A-2 cameras and overflights of the US, observed by Colonel Yancey, who certified readiness before a Pentagon panel. It recounts a 14 April 1956 double engine flameout over Tennessee, a glide to Kirtland AFB near Albuquerque (over 300 miles by glide), and the aircraft's fragility, high-altitude handling, and speed-control dangers.

nodes.title: THREE FATAL CRASHES IN 1956
nodes.summary: Describes three fatal or serious U-2 crashes in 1956. Rose stalled a U-2 after failing to shake loose a pogo during takeoff, and it disintegrated. On 31 August, Frank Grace stalled article 354 on a night takeoff and cartwheeled into a power pole. On 17 September, article 346 lost a wing after takeoff at Wiesbaden, killing Howard Carey. On 19 December, hypoxia impaired Robert Ericson, who exceeded speed limits and was ejected at 28,000 feet, surviving; article 357 was lost.

summary: Describes U-2 pilot training at March AFB under Col. William F. Yancey, with Lockheed test pilot Tony LeVier at Area 51, lacking a two-seat trainer for about 15 years. Covers flight limits (Mach 0.8), the 'coffin corner' airspeed band, vernier throttle, and celestial navigation accuracy under 1 nm per 1,000 nm. Covers Project AQUATONE's 31 U-2s, April 1956 final tests, a 14 April 1956 double flameout glide to Kirtland AFB, and aircraft fragility. Recounts three 1956 crashes: Rose's pogo-related stall, Grace's night stall, Carey's wing loss at Wiesbaden, and Ericson's hypoxia ejection.

title: COORDINATION OF COllECTION REQUIREMENTS
summary: Describes the establishment of the CIA's Ad Hoc Requirements Committee (ARC) in December 1955 under James Q. Reber to coordinate U-2 collection requirements. Covers its membership (CIA offices, Army, Navy, Air Force, later NSA and State Department), its role in prioritizing targets on Soviet long-range bombers, guided missiles, and nuclear energy, flight-plan justification, and differing agency interests, with consensus-seeking and occasional dissent.

title: PREPARATIONS TO HANDLE THE PRODUCT OF U-2 MISSIONS
summary: Describes CIA's preparations for U-2 photography: in Dec 1954 Dulles and Bissell briefed Lundahl, whose Photo-Intelligence Division created Project EQUINE. Staff grew from 13 to 44 in May 1955, moved to Que and then Steuart Buildings, and doubled in Jan 1956 with Project HTAUTOMAT. After April 1956 U-2 missions over US installations, the division was ready for U-2 operations starting summer 1956.

title: THE IMPACT OF THE AIR FORCE PROJECT GENETRIX BALLOONS
summary: Describes Air Force Project GENETRIX, which launched 516 camera balloons from Western Europe in 1956 over the USSR and China. Only 46 payloads were recovered and 34 yielded useful photos. The project caused diplomatic protests, and Eisenhower halted it. The photos were valuable baseline imagery. Balloon radar tracking gave wind data for U-2 flight planning, and the balloon's steel bar resonated with Soviet TOKEN radars, revealing them. CIA worried the protests would hurt U-2 overflights and the Free Europe balloon program.

title: AOUATONE BRIEFINGS FOR SELECTED MEMBERS OF CONGRESS
summary: Describes the AQUATONE briefings on the U-2 project. In February 1956, DCI Dulles told Senators Leverett Saltonstall and Richard B. Russell, the ranking Senate Armed Services members, about the highly secret project. They recommended briefing senior House committee members, such as John Taber, and Dulles later did so.

title: THE U-2 COVER STORY
summary: Describes the U-2 cover story: a weather research cover (NACA) was approved in March 1956, coordinated among Air Force, CIA, NACA (Dr. Hugh Dryden) and other agencies. Contingency plans were drafted for losing a U-2 over hostile territory, including pilot capture, with Bissell urging comprehensive action plans covering press releases, diplomacy, and worst-case scenarios. The policy to maintain the weather cover story even if captured later proved disastrous in May 1960.
